passage:
At the school water tap, Imran, five, was thirsty and pushed to the front. A girl in front of him stumbled. Rekha Ma'am crouched beside him. "Look, everyone is in a line, like an ant train. Your turn comes after Meena." Imran stood behind, counting under his breath: "One, two, three."
When it was his turn, Rekha Ma'am smiled. "You waited. That was hard, wasn't it? Well done." Imran drank and grinned, his cheeks wet.

qa.q: Whose turn comes before Imran's at the water tap?
qa.a: Imran's turn comes after Meena.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he pushed to the front?
qa.a: Imran was thirsty and impatient, so he pushed without thinking.

qa.q: What did Rekha Ma'am do that helped Imran learn to wait?
qa.a: She crouched beside him, compared the line to an ant train and named who was before him, then praised him when he waited.

qa.q: How might the girl who stumbled have felt?
qa.a: The girl was probably startled or upset at being pushed, which shows why taking turns matters to others.

grounding: A child pushes at the school water tap and learns to take turns with praise and clear examples.

passage: I'm Ganga, and my flat looks over the park. Yesterday Vijay, about five, shoved past two children on the slide steps. His grandmother did not shout. She knelt and said, "Look, they are waiting. Where does the line end?" Vijay pointed to the back and stood there, hopping from foot to foot, for three turns. When his turn came, his grandmother clapped. I don't know what he felt. But this morning I saw him wait at the steps again, tapping the rail, holding his place.

qa.q: What did Vijay's grandmother ask him?
qa.a: She asked, 'Where does the line end?'

qa.q: What might Vijay have been feeling while hopping from foot to foot in the line?
qa.a: He was probably impatient and eager for his turn, though the narrator says the exact feeling cannot be known.

qa.q: How did Vijay's grandmother help him learn to wait?
qa.a: She did not shout but knelt, asked where the line ended, and clapped when his turn came.

qa.q: How might the two children he pushed past have felt?
qa.a: They were probably surprised or cross at being shoved, which the line helps to avoid.

grounding: A child pushes at a slide and learns to take turns, with praise and a clear example.

passage:
"Arnab, wait! It's Riddhi's turn on the slide."
"But I want to go NOW!"
Arnab pushed forward. The little girl in front wobbled.
"Stop," said Vandana, crouching. "Look. There are four children. You're number five. Count with me."
"One, two, three, four... five."
"That's you. After four. Can you wait?"
Arnab scowled, then stood still. When his turn came, Vandana clapped. "You waited so well!"
He grinned and slid down, shouting, "I waited!"

qa.q: What number was Arnab in the line?
qa.a: Arnab was number five.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel when he pushed forward?
qa.a: Arnab felt impatient and wanted to go now.

qa.q: What helped Arnab learn to wait?
qa.a: Vandana calmly showed him his place by counting, then praised him when he waited.

qa.q: How might the little girl in front have felt when Arnab pushed?
qa.a: She probably felt scared and upset when she wobbled.

grounding: A young child pushes in the line for a slide, and a parent's clear example and praise help him learn to take turns.

passage:
Kindergarten teacher's note, Monday.
At the water tap after PE, Karthik, five, pushed past Varun and the others to drink first. Varun started to cry.
I asked Karthik to hold my hand and watch the line. "Who was first? Who was second?" He pointed. "Varun."
We drew a line of chalk footprints on the floor, one for each child. Karthik stood on his footprint and waited, bouncing on his toes. When he reached the tap, I said, "You waited your turn!" He beamed.
Later he told a younger child, "Stand on your footprint!"
Next step: I'll use footprints at the slide too.

qa.q: What did the teacher draw on the floor?
qa.a: The teacher drew a line of chalk footprints, one for each child.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel when he reached the tap?
qa.a: Karthik felt proud and pleased, beaming when praised.

qa.q: Why did the chalk footprints work?
qa.a: They gave clear, simple places to wait, and praise made taking turns feel good.

qa.q: How might Varun have felt when Karthik pushed past?
qa.a: Varun felt upset and hurt, which is why he started to cry.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a young child who pushed at the water tap learning to wait in line through clear examples and praise.

passage:
At the village fair, the swing had a long line of children. Kalyani, five, ran straight to the front.
"Kalyani, no," said her cousin Aadhya, who was nine. "See? We stand at the back."
Kalyani stamped her foot. "But I want it!"
Aadhya took her hand and walked her to the end of the line. "I'll wait with you. We'll count the swings."
They counted together. When Kalyani's turn came, the swing man said, "Good girl, you waited." Aadhya pushed her high. Kalyani laughed.

qa.q: Who took Kalyani to the end of the line?
qa.a: Her cousin Aadhya took her hand and walked her to the end of the line.

qa.q: How was Kalyani feeling when she stamped her foot?
qa.a: Kalyani felt impatient and cross, wanting the swing right away.

qa.q: What made Aadhya's help work?
qa.a: She showed Kalyani where to stand, waited with her and made counting a game, and the swing man's praise rewarded her.

qa.q: How might the other children have felt if Kalyani had stayed at the front?
qa.a: They might have felt it was unfair and upset, having waited their turn.

grounding: At a village fair, a young child tries to push to the front, and an older cousin's example and praise teach her to wait.

passage: At the park in Buenos Aires, Paulo ran to the slide and pushed past three children on the ladder. Alejandro wobbled and nearly fell. "Hey!" Paulo's mother called him down. "Look, Paulo. They were waiting. First Alejandro, then the girl in red, then the little one. Where do you go?" Paulo stamped. "I want it now!" "I know. Waiting is hard. You go at the end." He stood at the back, bouncing. When his turn came, his mother clapped. "You waited! That was hard, and you did it." Paulo slid down grinning and ran straight to the back of the line.

qa.q: Who nearly fell when Paulo pushed past?
qa.a: Alejandro wobbled and nearly fell.

qa.q: What was Paulo feeling when he stamped?
qa.a: Paulo felt impatient and cross, wanting the slide right away.

qa.q: What helped Paulo learn to take turns?
qa.a: His mother clearly showed the order, said that waiting is hard, and praised him warmly when he managed it.

qa.q: How might Alejandro have felt when Paulo pushed past?
qa.a: Alejandro was probably startled and scared when he wobbled, and upset that someone skipped his turn.

grounding: It illustrates a young child who pushes in line when impatient and learns to take turns through a clear example and praise.
